Now a princess named Moonlight... was smitten by the arrows of Love [for a passing prince], and said to her friend: "Dear girl, you must make an effort to bring us together this very day." ... But when night came, the prince thought it over [and refused to go, judging it dishonourable]. So after full reflection he did not go to her.

But Mister Duly was roaming through the night and spied a strap hanging down the wall of a fine stucco house. Out of curiosity mingled with bravado he took hold and climbed. Now the princess, being perfectly confident that he was the right man, treated him with high consideration... Then she went to bed with him... But she said: "...Why don't you realize this and talk to me?" And he replied: "What's duly his, a man receives." When she heard this, her heart stopped beating, and she sent him down the strap in a hurry.

So he made for a tumble-down temple and went to sleep. Presently a policeman... found him asleep... said: "This temple is deserted. Go and sleep in my bed." And he agreed, but made a blunder, lying down in the wrong bed [that of the policeman's daughter, Naughty, who mistook him for her own secret lover and married him by the ceremony used in heaven]... But she said: "Even yet you do not talk nicely with me. Why not?" And he replied: "What's duly his, a man receives." ... So she gave him a sorrowful scolding and sent him packing.

As he walked along a business street, there approached a bridegroom named Fine-Fame... At this moment an elephant reached the spot, running amuck... the crowd was in a hubbub... In this crisis Mister Duly perceived the girl [the bride], all alone, her eyes dancing with terror, and with the words: "Don't worry. I will save you," manfully reassured her, put his right arm around her, and with enormous sang-froid gave the elephant a cruel scolding. And the elephant - it was fate's doing - actually went away.

When the story got abroad... the princess... the policeman's daughter... and the king in turn... arrived at the spot... "Speak without apprehension. What sort of business is this?" And Mister Duly said: "What's duly his, a man receives." Then the princess remembered, and she said: "This law not even God can break." Then the policeman's daughter said: "My heart is not surprised, nor grieves." And the merchant's daughter said: "For what is mine, no strangers take."

Then the king promised immunity to one and all, arrived at the truth by piecing their narratives together, and ended by respectfully giving Mister Duly his own daughter, together with a thousand villages. Then he bethought himself that he had no son, so he anointed Mister Duly crown prince.

documents.curated_lesson: A weaver named Soft worked hard making fine garments, yet earned barely enough for food and clothes, while coarser weavers around him grew wealthy. Certain that a change of city would change his fortune, he set off for another land despite his wife's doubts about whether effort could really outrun destiny. After three years he started home with three hundred gold coins, but slept one night beneath a banyan tree and overheard two spirits arguing in his dream — one called Doer, one called Deed. Deed insisted that Soft was fated to have nothing beyond food and clothes; Doer replied that he was only bound to reward effort, and the outcome afterward was Deed's affair. Soft woke to find his gold bag empty. Undiscouraged, he earned five hundred gold coins the following year and took a different road home, only to find the very same tree, hear the very same argument, and wake to the very same empty bag. In despair, he prepared to end his life beneath that tree — until one of the spirits appeared and stopped him, revealing himself as the very Deed who took the gold, and offering Soft one wish in place of his lost fortune. Soft asked to understand wealth itself, and the spirit sent him to observe two merchants in the next city: one who hoarded everything fearfully and grew sick and friendless, and another who spent freely on gifts and hospitality and was rewarded by fortune again and again. Watching this, Soft understood what he truly wanted — not a pile of gold he could never touch, but the freedom to give. He asked to become the kind of person whose money flows outward in generosity rather than locked away, and from that day his life found its true wealth.
documents.source_name: The Panchatantra, translated by Arthur W. Ryder (1925)
documents.text:
In a certain town lived a weaver. His name was Soft, and he spent his time making garments dyed in various patterns, fit for such people as princes. But for all his labours, he could not collect a bit of money beyond food and clothes. Yet he saw other weavers, who made coarse fabrics, rolling in wealth, and he said to his wife: "...This city does not offer me a decent living. I am going to move." ... So he went to Growing City, stayed three years, and started home with savings of three hundred gold-pieces.

In mid-journey... he climbed upon a stout branch of a banyan tree and dozed. In the middle of the night... he heard two human figures... abusing each other. The first of them was saying: "Come now, Doer! ...you have, in every possible way, prevented this fellow Soft from getting any capital beyond food and clothes... Why did you give him three hundred gold pieces?" "Now, Deed!" said the other, "I am constrained to give the enterprising a reward in proportion to their enterprise. The final consequence is your affair. Take it from him yourself." On hearing this, Soft awoke and looked for his bag of gold [and found it empty].

So he made up his mind to return to Growing City. There he earned five hundred gold-pieces in just one single year, and started home again by a different road. When the sun went down, he came upon the very same banyan tree... he dozed off on a branch, and saw the same two figures [with the same argument, and] found [his bag] empty.

This plunged him into the depths of gloom, and he thought: "...I will just hang myself from this banyan tree and say goodbye to life." ...when one of the figures appeared in the sky and said: "Do not be so rash, Friend Soft. I am the person who takes your money... ask your heart's desire."

"In that case," said Soft, "give me plenty of money." "My good fellow," said the other, "what will you do with money which you cannot enjoy or give away? For you are to have no use of it beyond food and clothes." But Soft replied: "Even if I get no use of it, still I want it..."

"If things stand so," said the figure, "go once more to Growing City. There dwell two sons of merchants; their names are Penny-Hide and Penny-Fling. When you have observed their conduct, you may ask for yourself the nature of one or the other." With this he vanished.

[Soft visited Penny-Hide, a miser, who could not even feed him due to illness and expense; and then Penny-Fling, a generous spender, who fed and housed him well and was rewarded the very next morning with a gift of money from the king.]

When he saw this, Soft thought: "This Penny-Fling person, even without any capital, is a better kind of thing than that scaly old Penny-Hide. The proverb is right: The Scriptures' fruit is pious homes; Right conduct, that of learnèd tomes; Wives fructify in joy and son; And money's fruit is gifts and fun. So may the blessèd Lord of All make me a person whose money goes in gifts and fun. I see no good in Penny-Hiding." So the Lord of All took him at his word, making him that kind of person.

documents.curated_lesson: A powerful wild bull named Hang-Ball roamed the forest freely, and one day a jackal named Greedy and his wife noticed odd loose folds of flesh swinging beneath him as he walked to the river to drink. The wife jackal was certain these folds would fall off any day, and urged her husband to abandon their comfortable spot — where mice came reliably to drink — and follow the bull instead, so as not to miss the coming feast. Greedy doubted whether "someday" was worth giving up a sure thing today, but his wife pressed him with proverbs about boldness and effort, and reluctantly he agreed to follow the bull, telling himself the reward was surely close at hand. Season after season, year after year, the couple trailed the bull, watching those same folds sway and never fall, growing thinner themselves as they lived on scraps instead of their old reliable mouse-trail. In the fifteenth year, exhausted and no closer to their hoped-for feast, Greedy finally turned to his wife: whether these folds were loose or tight, falling or staying, they had watched them fifteen years for nothing — and it was time to go back to what had once fed them reliably.
documents.source_name: The Panchatantra, translated by Arthur W. Ryder (1925)
documents.text:
In a certain town lived a bull named Hang-Ball. From excess of male vigour he abandoned the herd, tore the river-banks with his horns, browsed at will on emerald-tipped grasses, and went wild in the forest.

In that forest lived a jackal named Greedy. One day he sprawled at ease with his wife on a sandy riverbank. At that moment the bull Hang-Ball came down to the same stretch of sand for a drink.

And the she-jackal said to her husband when she saw the hanging testicles: "Look, my dear! See how two lumps of flesh hang from that bull. They will fall in a moment, or a few hours at most. So you must follow him, please."

"My dear," said the jackal, "nobody knows. Perhaps they will fall some day, perhaps not. Why send me on a fool's errand? I would rather stay here with you and eat the mice that come to water..."

"Come," said she, "you are a coward, satisfied with any little thing... Besides, I am dreadfully tired of mouse-flesh, and these two lumps of meat are plainly on the point of falling. You must not refuse me."

So when he had listened to this, he left the spot where mice were to be caught and followed Hang-Ball... So he spent much time wandering with his wife after the bull. But they did not fall. At last in the fifteenth year, in utter gloom he said to his wife: "Loose they are, yet tight; Fall, or stick, my dear? I have watched them now Till the fifteenth year. Let us draw the conclusion that they will not fall in the future either, and return to the old mouse-trail."

documents.curated_lesson: A young fawn named Spot, only six months old and still not skilled at the herd's special escape-leap that older deer used to clear hunters' snares, wandered too far ahead one day and was caught in a trap while the rest of the herd escaped to safety. The hunter, moved by pity at the sight of so young a creature, spared his life and gave him as a gift to a prince, who kept Spot as a beloved pet — bathed, perfumed, fed delicacies, and passed fondly from hand to hand among the curious court. Despite every comfort, Spot never stopped missing the wild herd he had lost. One night in the rainy season, hearing thunder and watching lightning, his heart grew so full of longing that he recited a verse aloud, asking when he would run with the herd again, bracing against the wind. The prince, terrified to hear a voice from nowhere and thinking himself possessed by a demon, fled the room in disarray and offered a great reward to any healer who could cure him. A wise man who happened to be present understood at once and gently explained: it was only the deer, aching with homesickness in the rainy season, that had spoken — not a demon at all. Relieved and moved, the prince ordered Spot released back into the very forest he had come from.
documents.source_name: The Panchatantra, translated by Arthur W. Ryder (1925)
documents.text:
Long ago, when I was six months old, I used to gambol in front of all the rest, as a youngster does... Now we deer have two gaits, called the Jump-Up and the Straightaway. Of these I knew the Straightaway, but not the Jump-Up.

While amusing myself one day, I lost touch with the herd... Now they had avoided a snare by means of the Jump-Up; they stood in a body ahead of me, and waited, all looking at me. But I, ignorant of the Jump-Up, was caught in the hunter's snare.

When the hunter came up, he did not put me to death, for pity softened his heart at the thought: "He is a fawn, fit only for a pet." Instead, he carefully took me home and gave me as a plaything to a prince, who showed his delight at seeing me by giving the hunter a generous reward.

The prince treated me kindly, providing ointments, massage, baths, food, perfumes, and salves... Finally, one day in the rainy season, as the prince reclined on a couch, I observed the lightning, listened to the thunder, and, my heart wistful for my fondly remembered herd, I recited: "When shall I follow on the herd Of coursing deer again? When brace myself against the wind That whistles by? Ah, when?"

"Who said that?" cried the prince, and looked about him, terrified. When he saw me, he thought: "No man said it, but a deer. It is a prodigy. I am undone," and like one possessed by a devil, he tottered from the house... Thinking himself ridden by a demon, he tempted the sorcerers and magicians with a great reward.

Meanwhile, overhasty individuals were striking me with sticks, bricks, and cudgels, but... I was rescued by a certain holy man who said: "Why kill the poor beast?" ...he respectfully said to the prince: "Dear sir, in the rainy season he wistfully remembers his native herd, and therefore recited [the verse]."

On hearing this, the prince was cured of his feverish malady, returned to his normal state, and said to his men: "Douse the poor deer's head in plenty of water, and set him free in the forest he came from." And they did so.

documents.curated_lesson: Four Brahman friends, worn down by poverty, resolved to seek their fortune abroad. A wandering magician gave each of them a magic quill and told them to walk toward the Himalaya: wherever a man's quill dropped from his hand, treasure would be found beneath that very spot. The first man's quill fell where the soil was pure copper. Satisfied, he filled his bag and turned back, content with what he had. Walking on, the second man's quill fell over silver -- surely richer than copper -- and he too turned home, pleased with his gain. The third man's quill dropped over solid gold. His companion urged him onward, reasoning that if copper led to silver and silver to gold, something even greater must lie ahead. But the gold-finder had already found enough, and turned back satisfied, letting his friend go on alone. The last man pressed on alone through the scorching land until he found not gems, as he had hoped, but a man imprisoned by a whirling wheel of torment, cursed to bear it forever -- because he too had once asked the same greedy question the wrong way, without knowing when enough was enough. The moment he asked, the wheel leapt from that stranger's head onto his own, and only then did he understand the price of chasing "just a little more" without limit.
documents.source_name: The Panchatantra, translated by Arthur W. Ryder (1925)
documents.text:
In a certain town in the world were four Brahmans who lived as the best of friends. And being stricken with utter poverty, they took counsel together... "Let us at any cost strive to make money." ... So the magician [Terror-Joy] made four magic quills, and gave one to each, saying: "Go to the northern slope of the Himalaya Mountains. And wherever a quill drops, there the owner will certainly find a treasure."

Now as they followed his directions, the leader's quill dropped. And on examining the spot, he found the soil all copper. So he said: "Look here! Take all the copper you want." But the others said: "Fool! What is the good of a thing which, even in quantity, does not put an end to poverty? Stand up. Let us go on." And he replied: "You may go. I will accompany you no farther." So he took his copper and was the first to turn back.

The three others went farther. But they had traveled only a little way when the leader's quill dropped. And when he dug down, he found the soil all silver. At this he was delighted... "You two may go," said he. "I will not join you." So he took his silver and turned back.

The two went on until one quill dropped. When the owner dug down, he found the soil all gold. Seeing this, he was delighted... "Fool!" said the other. "Don't you see the point? First came copper, then silver, and then gold. Beyond there will certainly be gems. Stand up. Let us go farther." "You may go," he replied. "I will stay here and wait for you."

So the other went on alone. His limbs were scorched by the rays of the summer sun and his thoughts were confused by thirst... At last... he saw a man with blood dripping down his body; for a wheel was whirling on his head. Then he made haste and said: "Sir, why do you stand thus with a wheel whirling on your head? ...tell me if there is water anywhere. I am mad with thirst."

The moment the Brahman said this, the wheel left the other's head and settled on his own... And the fellow said: "When someone who holds in his hand a magic quill such as you had, arrives and speaks as you did, then it will settle on his head."

"My dear sir," said the fellow, "the god of wealth, fearful lest his treasures be stolen, prepared this terror, so that no magician might come so far. And if any should succeed in coming, he was to be freed from hunger and thirst, preserved from decrepitude and death, and was merely to endure this torture. So now permit me to say farewell. You have set me free from a sizable misery. Now I am going home." And he went.

documents.curated_lesson: In a pond lived two fish named Hundred-Wit and Thousand-Wit, along with their friend, a frog named Single-Wit. One evening they overheard fishermen planning to return at dawn with nets. Alarmed, the frog asked his friends whether they should flee that very night. Thousand-Wit laughed off the danger, boasting that his thousand tricks would surely save them. Hundred-Wit agreed, confident that a hundred clever schemes were more than enough. The frog admitted he had only a single idea, and it was simply to leave at once -- so that night, he and his wife swam away to another pond. At dawn the fishermen returned and swept the pond with their nets. Both clever fish, for all their boasted wit, were caught and carried away. From the safety of his new home, the frog watched the fishermen pass by carrying his two brilliant friends, and said quietly to his wife that a single wit, acted on in time, had outlasted a thousand clever tricks that were never used.
documents.source_name: The Panchatantra, translated by Arthur W. Ryder (1925)
documents.text:
In a certain pond lived two fishes whose names were Hundred-Wit and Thousand-Wit. And a frog named Single-Wit made friends with them.

One day at sunset they were engaged in conversation, when fishermen with nets came there, who said to one another on seeing the pond: "Look! This pond appears to contain plenty of fish... We will return at dawn." With this they went home.

The three friends felt this speech to be dreadful as the fall of a thunderbolt... The frog spoke first: "Hundred-Wit and Thousand-Wit, my dear friends, what should we do now: flee or stick it out?"

At this Thousand-wit laughed and said: "My good friend, do not be frightened merely because you have heard words... Yet should it take place, I will save you and myself by virtue of my wit. For I know plenty of tricks in the water." And Hundred-Wit added: "Yes, Thousand-Wit is quite right... You must not go away. I will save you by virtue of my wit."

"Well," said the frog, "I have only a single wit, and that tells me to flee. My wife and I are going to some other body of water this very night." So spoke the frog and under cover of night he went to another body of water.

At dawn the next day came the fish-catchers... and inclosed the pond with nets. And all the fishes, turtles, frogs, crabs, and other water-creatures were caught in the nets and captured. Even Hundred-Wit and Thousand-Wit fell into a net and were killed, though they struggled to save their lives by fancy turns.

On the following day the fishermen gleefully started home. One of them carried Hundred-Wit, who was heavy, on his head. Another carried Thousand-Wit tied to a cord. Then the frog, safe in the throat of a cistern, said to his wife: "Look, darling, look! While Hundred-Wit is on a head, While Thousand-Wit hangs limp and dead, Your humble Single-Wit, my dear, Is paddling in the water clear.

documents.curated_lesson: A donkey and a jackal, friends by night, would slip through a gap in the hedge into a farmer's cucumber field and feast together, always parting before dawn. One fine night, the donkey -- proud of his voice -- announced that he wished to sing. The jackal begged him to stay quiet. The donkey, offended at being called unmusical, launched into a long, proud explanation of the rules of classical music, insisting he was too cultured to be silenced. The jackal quietly stepped away to keep watch -- and the donkey brayed loudly across the field, exactly as the jackal had feared. The farmers woke at once, rushed out with clubs, beat the donkey soundly, and fastened a heavy mortar around his neck. As the battered donkey dragged himself away, the jackal called out with a smile: he had been offered fine advice and refused it, and now wore quite a "necklace" for his singing.
documents.source_name: The Panchatantra, translated by Arthur W. Ryder (1925)
documents.text:
In a certain town was a donkey named Prig. In the daytime he carried laundry packages, but was at liberty to wander anywhere at night. One night while wandering in the fields he fell in with a jackal and made friends. So the two broke through a hedge into cucumber-beds, and having eaten what they could hold of that comestible, parted at dawn to go home.

One night the egotistical donkey, standing among the cucumbers, said to the jackal: "See, nephew! The night is marvelously fine. I will contribute a song." "Don't, uncle," said the jackal. "It might make trouble, seeing that we are on thieves' business... Besides, your vocal music is not agreeable, since it resembles a blast on a conch-shell. The farmers would hear you from afar, would rise, and would fetter or kill you. Better keep quiet and eat."

"Come, come!" said the donkey. "Your remarks prove that you live in the woods and have no musical taste..." [The donkey recites an elaborate technical description of music theory to prove his qualifications.] "After this, how can you think me lacking in educated taste? How can you try to hinder me?"

"Very well, uncle," said the jackal. "I will stay by the gap in the hedge, and look for farmers. You may sing to heart's content." When he had done so, the donkey lifted his neck and began to utter sounds. But the farmers, hearing the bray of a donkey, angrily clenched their teeth, snatched cudgels, rushed in, and beat him so that he fell to the ground. Next they hobbled him by fastening on his neck a mortar with a convenient hole, then went to sleep.

Presently the donkey stood up... Then with the mortar on his neck, he trampled the hedge and started to run away. At this moment the jackal, looking on from a safe distance, said with a smile: "Well sung, uncle! Why would you Not stop when I told you to? What a necklace! Yes, you wear Music medals rich and rare." "Just so, you would not stop when I advised it.

documents.curated_lesson: A weaver named Slow, needing wood for his broken loom, raised his axe against a great tree by the sea -- only to discover it was home to a forest spirit, who begged him to spare it in exchange for any wish he desired. Before deciding, Slow consulted his friend the barber, who urged him to ask for a kingdom. But Slow insisted on asking his wife too. His wife thought the barber's idea foolish -- a kingdom brings only worry and rivalry. Instead she suggested that since one pair of hands already wove enough cloth to support them, an extra head and pair of arms would let him weave twice as much, doubling their income without any of a king's troubles. Delighted with this "sensible" plan, Slow asked the spirit for exactly that -- and instantly became two-headed and four-armed. But as he walked home rejoicing, the townspeople saw only a monstrous figure approaching and, terrified, beat him to death before he could explain himself.
documents.source_name: The Panchatantra, translated by Arthur W. Ryder (1925)
documents.text:
In a certain town lived a weaver named Slow. One day all the pegs in his loom broke. So he took an axe, and in his search for wood, came to the seashore. There he found a great sissoo tree, and he thought: "This seems a good-sized tree. If I cut it down, I can make plenty of weaving-tools." He therefore lifted his axe upon it.

Now there was a fairy in the tree who said: "My friend, this tree is my home. Please spare it..." "Sir," said the fairy, "I have taken a liking to you. Ask anything you like, but spare this tree." "In that case," said the weaver, "I will go home and return after asking my friend and my wife."

...he encountered his particular friend, the barber, and said: "My friend, I have won the favor of a fairy. Tell me what to ask for." And the barber said: "My dear fellow... ask for a kingdom. You can be king, and I will be prime minister..." "Quite so, my friend," replied the weaver. "However, I shall ask my wife, too." "Don't," said the barber. "It is a mistake to consult women..."

And the weaver rejoined: "You may be right. Still, I shall ask her. She is a good wife." ...he said to her: "...I have come to ask you to tell me what to say to him. Here is my friend, the barber, who tells me to ask for a kingdom." "Dear husband," said she, "what sense have barbers? Do not take his advice... this king-business means a series of dreadful troubles..."

"Yes," said the weaver, "you are right. But tell me what to ask for." And she replied: "As it is, you turn out one piece of cloth a day, and this meets all our expenses. Now ask for a second pair of arms and an extra head, so that you may produce one piece of cloth in front and another behind. The price of one meets the household expenses, with the price of the other you may put on style..."

...he was delighted and said: "Splendid, my faithful wife! You have made a splendid suggestion. I am determined to follow it." So the weaver went and laid his request before the fairy: "...pray give me a second pair of arms and an extra head." And in the act of speaking he became two-headed and four-armed.

But as he came home, delight in his heart, the people thought he was a fiend, and beat him with clubs and stones and things so that he died.

documents.curated_lesson: A king kept a troupe of pet monkeys for his son's amusement, alongside a herd of rams. One greedy ram kept raiding the palace kitchen, and the cooks regularly drove him off. The eldest monkey saw the danger: if the cooks ever struck the ram with a burning stick, he might catch fire, stampede into the stable, and burn the horses -- and monkey-fat was the prescribed remedy for burned horses. He urged the troupe to leave for the forest at once, but the others laughed at his fear and refused. Unwilling to watch his family come to harm, the old monkey left alone. Soon after, exactly as he had feared, the burning ram fled into the stable, the horses were burned, and the king's physicians prescribed monkey-fat -- so every monkey left behind was killed. When the old monkey learned what had happened, he found a lake guarded by a man-eating spirit and struck a bargain: in exchange for a pearl necklace, he lured the same king and his retinue to the lake with tales of treasure, letting the spirit take them as they entered the water, while sparing the king himself with a final warning about what his cruelty had cost.
documents.source_name: The Panchatantra, translated by Arthur W. Ryder (1925)
documents.text:
In a certain city was a king named Moon, who had a pack of monkeys for his son's amusement... For the amusement of the same prince there was a herd of rams. One of them had an itching tongue, so he went into the kitchen at all hours of the day and night and swallowed everything in sight. And the cooks would beat him with any stick or other object within reach.

Now when the chief of the monkeys observed this, he reflected: "Dear me! This quarrel between ram and cooks will mean the destruction of the monkeys... Suppose some time they find nothing else and beat him with a firebrand. Then that broad, woolly back will very easily catch fire. And if the ram, while burning, plunges into the stable near by, it will blaze... and the horses will be scorched. Now the standard work on veterinary science prescribes monkey-fat to relieve burns on horses..." Having reached this conclusion, he assembled the monkeys [and urged them to flee to the forest].

But the conceited monkeys laughed at his warning... Having listened to this, the monkey chief... said: "...I will not behold the death of my household. I am off for that very forest." With these words the chief left them all behind, and went to the forest.

One day after he had gone, the ram entered the kitchen. And the cook, finding nothing else, picked up a firebrand, half-consumed and still blazing, and struck him. Whereat, with half his body blazing, he plunged bleating into the stable near by. There he rolled until flames started up on all sides... and of the horses tethered there some died... In this state of affairs, the saddened king assembled the veterinary surgeons... they said: "...Let monkey-fat be freely used..." When the king heard this, he ordered the slaughter of the monkeys. And, not to waste words, every one was killed.

Now the monkey chief did not with his own eyes see this outrage... But he heard the story as it passed from one to another, and did not take it tamely... Now as the elderly monkey wandered about thirsty, he came to a lake... he noticed footprints leading into the lake, but none coming out... there issued from the water a man-eating fiend with a pearl necklace adorning his neck, who spoke and said: "Sir, I eat everyone who enters the water... I have taken a liking to you. Name your heart's desire."

"And I," said the monkey, "I live in mortal enmity with a king. If you will give me that pearl necklace, I will awaken his greed with a plausible narrative, and will make that king enter the lake along with his retinue." So the fiend handed over the pearl necklace.

[The monkey then lures the king and his court to the lake with tales of a magic pearl-granting lake.] So the king and his retinue started, greedy for pearl necklaces... So all the attendants entered and were eaten by the fiend. Then, as they lingered, the king said to the monkey: "Well, chief, why do my attendants linger?" And the monkey hurriedly climbed a tree before saying to the king: "You villainous king, your attendants are eaten by a fiend that lives in the water. My enmity with you, arising from the death of my household, has been brought to a happy termination. Now go. I did not make you enter there, because I remembered that you were the king..."

When the king heard this, he hastened home, grief-stricken.

documents.curated_lesson: A fiend haunted a princess every evening, unable to carry her off because she protected herself with a magic circle. One night, overhearing her complain about "the one who torments me every evening at twilight," the fiend mistook this for the name of a rival -- someone called Twilight, more powerful than himself. Anxious to learn what this rival looked like, the fiend took the form of a horse and slipped into the royal stables. That night, a horse-thief crept in, chose the disguised fiend, and rode off on him. Every tug of the reins convinced the terrified fiend that "Twilight" himself was punishing him. He bolted in panic, while the thief, equally alarmed that this horse obeyed no rein, clung on until he could grab a tree branch and escape. A monkey friend of the fiend mocked him for running from a mere man, and the fiend, embarrassed, turned back to attack -- but the thief, now furious, seized the monkey's dangling tail in his teeth and bit down hard, and the monkey, mistaking this for an even more terrifying force, froze in silent terror.
documents.source_name: The Panchatantra, translated by Arthur W. Ryder (1925)
documents.text:
In a certain city lived a king whose name was Fine-Army. He had a daughter named Pearl... Now a certain fiend, who wished to carry her off, came every evening and abused her, but he could not carry her off because she protected herself by drawing a magic circle.

While matters were in this state, the fiend once... revealed himself to the princess, who thereupon said to a girl friend: "Look, my dear! This is the fiend who comes every evening at twilight's hour and torments me. Is there any means of keeping the ruffian at a distance?"

When he heard this, the fiend thought: "Aha! I am not the only one. There is someone else -- and his name is Twilight -- who comes every day to carry her off. But he cannot do it either. Suppose I take the form of a horse, go to the stable, and find out what he looks like and what power he has."

When he had done so, a horse-thief came to the palace at dead of night. He examined all the horses, found the fiend-horse the finest, put a bit in his mouth, and mounted. Meanwhile the fiend was thinking: "I presume this is the fellow named Twilight. He thinks me a vile creature, he is angry, he has come to kill me. What shall I do?"

While he was thinking, the horse-thief struck him with a whip. And he was terrified and started to run. The thief, for his part, after traveling some distance, tried to stop him by tugging at the bit... he reflected: "Well, well! Horses are not like this. This must be a fiend in equine form. So if I find a spot thick with dust, I will drop. It is my one chance of life."

...the fiend-horse passed under a banyan tree. And the thief caught a branch and stuck. So both of them gained the hope of life from their separation... Now in the banyan was a monkey, a friend of the fiend, who said when he saw the fiend making off: "Look here! Why do you run from an imaginary danger? This is your natural food, a man. Eat him."

On hearing this, the fiend took his own form and turned about... And when the thief saw that the monkey had called him back, he was angry. As the monkey sat above, and his tail hung down, the thief took it in his mouth and started to chew very hard. Then the monkey concluded that he was dealing with one more powerful than the fiend, and was too frightened to utter a word.

documents.curated_lesson: A king's newborn daughter carried a rare mark that the customs of the land considered a grave misfortune. His counselor advised consulting scholars, who ruled that she must be married off to whoever would have her, and both then exiled. A drum was sounded announcing gold and a bride to anyone willing to marry her and leave. A blind man, guided by a hunchbacked companion, accepted the offer for the gold, reasoning that even hardship was better than the poverty they knew. The three settled in a distant town. Over time, resentment grew between the hunchback and the princess against the blind man who depended so heavily on them, and the two began plotting to be rid of him. Their scheme unraveled in confusion: in the middle of carrying it out, the blind man's sight was accidentally restored by fumes he had not expected, and in the struggle that followed, the impact that was meant to harm him instead straightened the hunchback's back and smoothed away the mark the princess had carried since birth. What was set in motion as betrayal ended, by chance, correcting every one of the misfortunes that had brought the three of them together in the first place.
documents.source_name: The Panchatantra, translated by Arthur W. Ryder (1925)
documents.text:
In the north country was a city called Honey-Town, where the king was named Honey-Host. And once there was born to him a daughter with three breasts. As soon as he learned of the birth of a three-breasted girl, he summoned the chamberlain and said: "Sir, let this girl be exposed in the forest, so that not a single soul may learn the fact."

To this the chamberlain replied: "O king of kings, it is a well-known fact that a three-breasted daughter brings misfortune. In spite of this, the Brahmans should be summoned and their opinion asked, in order that no law be offended..." [The chamberlain illustrates this principle with the embedded tale "The Fiend Who Washed His Feet."]

After listening to this, the king summoned the Brahmans... And they replied: "O King, listen. A daughter fitted out with limbs Too numerous or few, Will lose her character... But if the father sees a girl With triple breast about, She dooms him to a speedy death... Therefore, O King, shun the sight of her. Give her to anyone who will marry her, but banish him from the country."

...he ordered a proclamation... "There is a three-breasted princess. To anyone who marries her the king will give a hundred thousand gold-pieces, but will exile him." For a long time this proclamation was made without anyone marrying the princess...

Now there was a blind man in the city, and as companion he had a hunchback named Slow, who guided him with a staff. These two heard the drum and consulted... "In case we touch that drum, we get girl and gold... even if death results from the girl's deformity, it will put a final end to the wretchedness of poverty."

...the blind man went and touched the drum, saying: "I will marry the girl." ...the king's men... took the three-breasted princess to the river-bank, married her to the blind man, and gave him the hundred thousand gold-pieces... [they were sent] to a foreign land.

...There in a certain town they purchased a house and lived comfortably. The blind man, however, spent all his time dozing on a couch. The hunchback did the housework. In course of time the princess had an intrigue with the hunchback, and she said: "My beloved, if this blind man happened to be killed, we should live happily together. Please find some poison..."

...the hunchback picked up a dead black snake... "Please cut it up, season it... and give it to that eyeless fellow, telling him it is fish. Then he will die in a hurry." ...she cut up the snake, put it in a kettle with buttermilk, placed it over the fire... she civilly said to the blind man: "...please take the spoon and stir them." ...he was delighted... took the spoon, and started to stir.

But as he did so, the poisoned steam reached his eyes, and the film began to peel off... his vision cleared and looking into the kettle, he saw nothing but chopped black snake... he concealed his feelings and behaved like a blind man. Presently Slow returned and without hesitation began to hug the wife... And the blind man saw it all.

Not finding a knife, he went up to Slow in the old way, wrathfully seized him by the feet, whirled him about his head with every bit of strength he could muster, and dashed him against the chest of the three-breasted woman. And the blow from the hunchback's body forced the third breast in, while the hunchback, when his hump smashed against her bosom, became straight.

documents.story_title: The Fiend Who Washed His Feet
documents.curated_lesson: A fiend seized a Brahman in the forest, climbed onto his shoulders, and ordered him to walk on. The frightened Brahman noticed the fiend's feet were unusually soft. When asked why, the fiend explained he was bound by a vow never to let his feet touch the ground unwashed. They came to a lake, and the fiend told the Brahman to wait while he bathed and completed his worship. The Brahman understood what awaited him once the fiend returned, and also understood that, bound by his own vow, the fiend would not dare set his unwashed feet on the ground to chase him. So the moment the fiend entered the water, the Brahman ran for his life -- and true to his word, the fiend did not follow. The very discipline the fiend had imposed on himself became the one weakness that set his intended victim free.
documents.source_name: The Panchatantra, translated by Arthur W. Ryder (1925)
documents.text:
In a certain forest lived a fiend named Cruel. One day he met a Brahman in his wanderings, climbed on his shoulder, and said: "Now go ahead."

So the terrified Brahman started off with him. But on observing that the fiend's feet were soft as a lotus-heart, he asked him: "Sir, why are your feet so tender?" And the fiend replied: "I am under a vow never to touch the ground with my feet until I have washed them."

Soon the Brahman, while meditating a plan of escape, came to a lake. Here the fiend said: "Sir, do not stir from this spot until I come forth from the lake after bathing and worshiping the god."

Thereupon the Brahman thought: "He will be sure to eat me after his worship. I will hurry away. For he will not follow me with unwashen feet." And when he did so, the fiend, not daring to break his vow, did not follow.

"And that is why I say: A prudent man should always ask, and the rest of it.

documents.curated_lesson: A frog-king named Theodore, tormented by his own relatives in the well where he lived, resolved on a plan of revenge: he would invite a black snake named Handsome into the well to destroy them all. The snake was wary at first, but Theodore's promise of a safe hiding place and an effortless meal won him over. Theodore led him into the well and pointed out which relatives to eat, believing he could control exactly how far the revenge would go. The snake ate every relative Theodore pointed to, then every friend besides -- and when the well was finally empty of victims, he calmly informed Theodore that he had no way to leave, and this well would be his home from here on, fed by one frog a day, even from Theodore's own family, or he would eat everyone at once. When at last only Theodore remained, the snake asked for his final meal. Theodore, given one chance to leave and search for more frogs elsewhere, simply did not return.
documents.source_name: The Panchatantra, translated by Arthur W. Ryder (1925)
documents.text:
There was once a frog-king in a well, and his name was Theodore. One day when tormented by his relatives, he climbed from bucket to bucket up the water-wheel, and finally emerged. Then he thought: "How can I pay those relatives back?"... With this in mind, he saw a black snake named Handsome crawling out of his hole. And on seeing him, he thought once more: "I will invite that black snake into the well, and clean out all my relatives."

Having come to this conclusion, he went to the mouth of the hole and called: "Come out! Come out, Handsome! Come out!" But when the snake heard this, he thought: "Whoever he may be that is calling me, he does not belong to my race... So I will just stay here until I am sure who he may be."

So he said: "Who are you?" The other said: "I am a frog-king named Theodore, and I have come to make friends with you." When the snake heard this, he said: "Why, it is incredible. Does grass make friends with fire?" But Theodore said: "You are quite right, sir. You are my born enemy. And yet I come to you because I have been insulted... My relatives [insulted me]."

"But," said the snake, "I can't get in [to the well]. And if I could, there is no place for me to lie while killing your relatives." But Theodore replied: "No, sir. Come with me. I will show you an easy way into the well. And inside there is a very attractive hole at water-level. There you can lie, and you will find it child's play to finish my relatives."

Then the snake reflected: "Yes, I am old. Now and then, with great effort, I catch one mouse. And often I don't..." After these reflections, he said: "Well, Theodore, if you really mean it, lead the way. We will go together." ... "Friend Handsome," said Theodore, "I will take you there by an easy way and show you the resting-place. But you must spare my family. You must not eat any except those I point out." "My dear fellow," said the snake, "you and I are now friends. Have no fear. I will do nothing but what you wish."

Then he came out of his hole, hugged the frog, and started off with him... Then Theodore settled the black snake in the hole and showed him the relatives. And he ate them all one after another. And lacking relatives, he made up to a few of the friends, and ate them, too.

Then the snake said: "My dear fellow, I have disposed of your enemies. Please give me something to eat, for you brought me here." "But, my dear fellow," said Theodore, "you have done what a friend should do. Pray return by way of the buckets." "Friend Theodore," said Handsome, "you make a serious mistake. How can I go home? My hole was my fortress, and it is surely occupied by strangers. Here I stay, and you must give me a frog at a time, even from your own family. If not, I will eat everyone."

At this, Theodore was disturbed in spirit... So he made up his mind, and assigned a frog a day. And the snake ate this one and another, too, behind the frog-king's back... Now one day, while eating frogs, he ate a frog named Theodosius, the son of Theodore. And Theodore, seeing him do it, wailed with piercing shrillness.

Now in course of time the frogs were finished one and all; only Theodore remained. And then Handsome said: "My dear Theodore, I am hungry and all the frogs are finished. Please give me something to eat, for you brought me here." Theodore said: "My friend, feel no anxiety on that head while I am alive. If you permit me to leave, I will persuade the frogs in other wells, and bring them all here." The snake said: "Well, I can't eat you, for you are like a brother. Now if you do as you say, you will be like a father."

So the frog planned his escape, and left the well, while Handsome waited there, impatient for his return... [Handsome sends a lizard to plead with Theodore to return.] But Theodore said: "The hungry man at nothing sticks; The poor man has his heartless tricks. Tell Handsome, miss, that Theodore Will see him in the well no more." And so he sent her back.

documents.curated_lesson: A lion, badly wounded and too weak to hunt, sent his jackal servant Dusty to find easy prey. Dusty came upon a donkey named Flop-Ear, worn thin by an unkind master. Sensing the donkey's loneliness, Dusty spun a story of a lush meadow full of gentle company, and even invented unmarried she-donkeys eager for a husband. Flop-Ear agreed at once and followed him to the lion's hiding place, but the weakened lion sprang too soon and missed, and the terrified donkey fled home. Dusty tracked him down again with an even more elaborate story -- that the frightening creature had been a lovesick she-donkey threatening to harm herself if Flop-Ear didn't return. Persuaded again, Flop-Ear returned, and this time the lion did not miss. The jackal then ate the best parts before the lion returned, talking his way out of the theft with a clever excuse.
documents.source_name: The Panchatantra, translated by Arthur W. Ryder (1925)
documents.text:
There was once a lion named Fierce-Mane, who lived in a part of a forest. And for servant he had a jackal, a faithful drudge named Dusty. Now one day the lion fought with an elephant, and took such cruel wounds on his body that he could not stir a foot... "My good Dusty," said the lion, "hunt out some animal that I can kill even in my present state."

So the jackal went hunting... he saw beside a tank a donkey named Flop-Ear who was choking over the thin and prickly grass. And he drew near and said: "Uncle, my respects to you..." And Flop-Ear answered: "What am I to do, nephew? The laundryman is merciless, and tortures me with dreadful burdens..."

"Well, uncle," said the jackal, "I know a lovely spot by a river, all covered with emerald grass. Come there and live with me..." "Very well said, nephew," answered Flop-Ear, "but village beasts are likely to be killed by forest animals..." "No, no," said the jackal. "My paws form a cage to protect the spot... Besides, there are three unmarried she-donkeys who were tormented just like you by laundrymen. They have now grown plump; they are young and frisky; they said to me: 'Uncle dear, go to some village and bring us a proper husband.'..."

Now when he heard the jackal's words, Flop-Ear felt his limbs quiver with love, and he said: "In that case, my dear sir, lead the way. We will hurry there."... So the poor creature went with the jackal into the lion's presence. But the lion was dreadfully foolish. When he saw the donkey actually within range of his spring, he was so overjoyed that he jumped over him and landed on the other side... he saw the egregious creature, cruel, horrifying, with bloodshot eyes, and he beat a hasty, terrified retreat to his own city.

Then the jackal said to the lion: "Well, what does this mean? I saw your heroic exhibition." And the lion was dumfounded... "My dear fellow," said the lion, "he saw me face to face and escaped. How can he be enticed here again? Bring me some other animal." But the jackal said: "Why should you worry about that? I am wide awake on that point." So the jackal followed the donkey's tracks, and found him grazing in the old place.

...Then the jackal laughed and said: "Uncle, that was a she-donkey. She was unspeakably lovesick, and seeing you, she rose up passionately to embrace you. But you were shy, and ran away... So come back. She has resolved to starve to death for your sake, and she says: 'If Flop-Ear does not marry me, I will plunge into fire or water, or will eat poison...' So have mercy, and return..."

So the donkey, persuaded by this reasoning, started off with him once more... Thereupon the donkey, deceived by a hundred arguments of the rascal, came again into the presence, and was straightway killed by the lion, who had prepared his spring beforehand. And then the lion set the jackal on guard, and went himself to the river to bathe. Whereupon the greedy jackal ate the donkey's ears and heart.

Now when the lion returned... he found the donkey minus ears and heart, and his soul was suffused with wrath, and he said to the jackal: "You scoundrel! What is this unseemly deed?..." "O King," said the jackal respectfully, "do not speak so. This creature was born without ears and heart. Otherwise, how could he have come here, have seen you with his own eyes, have run in terror, and then come back?..." So the lion was convinced by the jackal's argument, divided with him, and ate his own share without suspicion.

documents.story_title: The Jackal Who Killed No Elephants
documents.curated_lesson: A lion, finding a baby jackal alone on the trail, could not bring himself to kill so young a creature, and brought him home alive to the lioness. She too refused to feed on a baby, and raised him as her own third son alongside her twin lion cubs. The three grew up together until a wild elephant wandered near and the lion cubs charged at it eagerly. The jackal, understanding the danger they did not, warned them off and ran for home himself. The twins, seeing only that their brother had fled, mocked him mercilessly. Wounded pride overtook the jackal's good judgment, and he declared he would kill them both to prove his courage. The lioness finally told him gently what she had always known: he was born a jackal, not a lion, and no amount of pride could change what fighting an elephant would cost him. She sent him off to rejoin his own kind before his wounded pride could destroy him.
documents.source_name: The Panchatantra, translated by Arthur W. Ryder (1925)
documents.text:
In a part of a forest lived a lion and his wife. One day the lioness gave birth to twins. And the lion killed deer and things every day, and gave them to the lioness. But one day as he ranged the forest, he had met nothing when the blessèd sun sank to his setting. As he trotted home, he found a baby jackal on the trail. And he pitied it because it was a baby. So he held it between his teeth and carefully carried it home, giving it to the lioness alive.

Then the lioness said: "Have you brought any food, sweetheart?" And he answered: "My dear, I didn't find a thing today except this jackal cub. Even him I did not kill, for I thought: 'He is a creature much like us, and a baby at that.'... Now suppose you eat him... In the morning I will bring something else." "Sweetheart," said she, "you did not kill him because you thought: 'He is a baby.' So how can I destroy him for my belly's sake?... So he shall be my third son." After this reply, she gave him her own milk and made him very fat. So the three cubs spent their babyhood in the same business and amusements, not recognizing any difference in parentage.

Now one day a wild elephant came wandering into that forest. The two lion-cubs, when they saw him, wrathfully started for him, eager to kill. But the jackal-cub said: "Brothers, that is an elephant, an enemy of your race. Don't go near him." With this he ran home. And the other two, seeing their elder brother routed, felt their pluck ooze away.

Later the twin brothers went home, and humorously told their parents how their elder brother had behaved. "Why, you know," said they, "the minute he saw him, he couldn't get far enough quick enough." When the jackal heard this, wrath entered his spirit... And he spoke harshly, scolding the twins. Then the lioness took him aside and admonished him: "You must never, never speak so, my dear. They are your brothers." But her patient pleading filled him with greater anger, and he burst upon her, too: "Do you think me their inferior in courage or beauty or science or application or skill? What right have they to ridicule me? I am certainly going to kill them."

When she heard this outburst, the lioness laughed quietly - for she did not wish him to die - and said: "Handsome you are, and valorous; You have a scholar's brain: But in your family, my boy, No elephants are slain. Now listen carefully, my dear. Your mother was a jackal, and I fattened you with my own milk because I pitied you. Now while my twins are babies and do not know you for a jackal, hurry away and join your own people. If not, they will fight you, and you will tread the path of death." When the jackal heard this, he was terror stricken, and softly stole away to join his own people.

documents.curated_lesson: A Brahman, devoted to his wife despite constant family conflict, left home with her. When she died of thirst in a forest, a heavenly voice offered him a way to save her: give up half of his own remaining life through a sacred vow. He did so, and she rose alive. But the second chance simply revealed who she already was: she fell for a crippled stranger, secured his devotion through a manipulative threat, and maneuvered her husband into carrying the stranger along in a basket. At a well, she and her new companion pushed the Brahman in and left him for dead, then presented themselves to a king as a devoted wife who had carried her disabled husband to safety, and was rewarded with land and honor. The Brahman survived and eventually reached the same city, where his wife denounced him to the king as an impostor. Facing execution, the Brahman asked only that she return what belonged to him -- the half-life he had given her. Forced to repeat the sacred words in front of the king, she fell dead on the spot.
documents.source_name: The Panchatantra, translated by Arthur W. Ryder (1925)
documents.text:
There was once a Brahman in a certain city who loved his wife more than his life. But she squabbled with his family every day, and never rested. Since he could not endure the squabbling, yet was devoted to his wife, he left his family and started for another country far away.

In the middle of a great forest, the Brahman's wife said: "My dear, I am tortured by thirst. Please look about for water." And he did as she requested, but when he returned with water, he found her dead. Since he loved her dearly, he fell into despair, but as he lamented, he heard a voice from heaven, saying: "Brahman, if you will give half your own life, your wife may live." So he performed a ceremony of purification, then gave a half of his own life by repeating the three magic words: "I give life." The moment he spoke, his wife stood up, alive.

So together they drank the water, ate forest fruits, and started on. Finally, they entered a flower garden near a city, where the Brahman said to his wife: "Belovèd, please stay here until I return with food." And he left her. Now in the garden was a cripple, turning a waterwheel and singing with a heavenly voice. When she heard the song, she was smitten with love, went to him, and said: "Dear friend, if you do not give me your love, you will be the murderer of a Brahman woman." ...she said: "From this moment I give you my person for life. You must accompany us with this understanding."

Then when the Brahman returned with food and began to eat with her, she said: "This cripple is hungry. Please give him a bite, too."... the lady said: "Brahman, when you go alone to another village, I have no one to talk to. Suppose we take this cripple with us." But he replied: "I cannot even carry myself, to say nothing of this cripple." "I will carry him," said she, "if he will get into a basket." And the Brahman agreed, his judgement being bewildered by her artful argument.

One day thereafter, as they rested near a well, the wife, aided by the cripple, gave the Brahman a push and plunged him in. And she took the cripple and went to a city. There the policemen... snatched [the basket] from her, and took it to the king. And as soon as the king had it opened, he saw the cripple. Presently the Brahman's wife arrived, weeping and wailing... And when the king asked, "What does this mean?" she said: "This is my invalid husband who was tormented by countless relatives, until, distracted by love, I put him on my head and brought him before you." And the king said: "You are my sister. Receive two villages, enjoy their delights with your husband, and make yourself comfortable."

At this point the Brahman arrived in the same city, for a certain holy man, as it happened, had drawn him from the well... When the wicked wife saw him, she denounced him to the king. "O King," she said, "there comes my husband's enemy." And the king sentenced him to death. But the Brahman said: "Your Majesty, this woman has something which she received from me. If you love justice, make her give it back." "My good woman," said the king, "restore whatever you may have that belongs to him." And she replied: "Your Majesty, I have nothing." Then the Brahman said: "With three magic words I gave you half my life. Give me that." And from fear of the king she murmured, just as he had done, the three words "I give life," and fell dead.

Then the king was amazed and said: "What does this mean?" And the Brahman related to him all that had gone before. "And that is why I say: I left my family for her; I gave her half my life; She leaves me now without a thought; What man can trust his wife?"

documents.curated_lesson: Splendour, secretary to King Joy and a master of every branch of scholarship, found himself utterly unable to out-argue his wife's temper during a quarrel. When she demanded he shave his head and bow at her feet as the price of forgiveness, he did exactly that. The next morning, freshly shaved, he appeared before the king, who openly teased him for his strange appearance -- unaware his own wife had grown just as displeased with him. Devoted to his own household peace, the king agreed to take a bit in his mouth, let his wife ride him like a horse, and neigh on command, simply to win back her favor. When Splendour later witnessed the king in his own moment of comic devotion, he could only reflect, wryly, that no learning or rank shields anyone from doing foolish things for love.
documents.source_name: The Panchatantra, translated by Arthur W. Ryder (1925)
documents.text:
There was once a king named Joy, lord of the sea-girdled earth... He had a secretary named Splendour, who had absorbed the total truth of all the scientific textbooks, but whose wife pouted in a lovers' quarrel. "Belovèd," said her husband, "tell me the means of appeasing you. I will adopt it without fail." And it cost her a struggle to say: "If you will shave your head and fall at my feet, then I will think of relenting." When he did so, she did so.

Now Joy's wife became angry in just the same way, and would not be appeased though he begged her pardon. Then he said: "Beloved, I cannot live a moment without you. I will fall at your feet and beg your pardon." She said: "If you hold a bit in your mouth and let me climb on your back and drive you, and if, when driven, you neigh like a horse, then I will relent." And this was done.

Next morning Splendour came before the king as he sat in council. And the king asked, when he saw him: "Good Splendour, why is your head shaved at this odd time?" And Splendour answered: "What will not man for woman do, When heads are shorn - at odd times, too? What will not man for woman say, When those who are not horses, neigh?"

documents.curated_lesson: A farmer's wife, restless in her marriage to a much older husband, was drawn in when a smooth-talking rogue professed sudden love for her. He proposed that if she brought her husband's savings, they could run off together. She agreed, gathered every coin, and met the rogue at dawn. As they neared a river, the rogue began calculating the cost of keeping her around. Under the pretense of carrying the money safely across first, he took everything, then asked for her clothes too, and simply walked away with it all, leaving her alone and stripped of everything. As she sat grieving on the riverbank, she watched a hungry jackal nearby lose her own meal in almost the same way -- distracted by a leaping fish, the jackal dropped the meat she carried, only for a vulture to steal it, while the fish escaped in the confusion. When the woman mocked the jackal for losing both fish and meat through her own carelessness, the jackal turned the same observation back on her with equal sharpness: the woman herself had lost both husband and lover, sitting exposed and alone by the same river.
documents.source_name: The Panchatantra, translated by Arthur W. Ryder (1925)
documents.text:
There was once a farmer who lived with his wife in a certain place. And because the husband was old, the wife was forever thinking of lovers... Now a rogue who lived by pilfering, noticed her and said: "You lovely creature, my wife is dead, and I am smitten with love at the sight of you. Pray enrich me with love's perfect treasure." And she said: "You beautiful man, if you feel that way, my husband has a great deal of money... I will bring it, so that I may go somewhere with you..."

Then at night, while her husband slept, she took all the money, and reached the rendezvous at dawn. The rogue, for his part, put her in front, started south, and travelled two leagues... But when he saw a river ahead, he reflected: "What am I to do with this middle-aged female?... I will just take her money and be off." So he said to her: "My dear, this is a great river, hard to cross. I will just take the money and put it safe on the far bank, then return to carry you alone on my back..." "Do so, my beloved," said she.

So he took the money to the last penny, and then he said: "Dearest, hand me your dress and your wrap, too, so that you may travel through the water unembarrassed." And when she did so, the rogue took the money and the two garments and went to the place he had in mind.

Then the farmer's wife sat down woebegone on the river-bank... At that moment a she-jackal came to the spot, carrying a piece of meat. As she came up and peered about, a great fish leaped from the water and was stranded on the bank. On spying him, she dropped the meat and darted at the fish. Whereupon a vulture swooped from the sky and flew off with the meat. And the fish, perceiving the jackal, struggled into the river. So the she-jackal had her pains for nothing, and as she gazed after the vulture, the naked woman smiled and said: "You poor she-jackal! The vulture has your meat; The water holds your fish: Of fish and flesh forlorn, What further do you wish?"

And the she-jackal, perceiving that the woman was equally forlorn, having lost her husband's money and her lover, said with a sneer: "You naked thing! Your cleverness is twice As great as mine, it would seem; Lover and husband lost, You sit beside the stream."

documents.curated_lesson: A hen-sparrow, nested comfortably in a tree, watched a monkey take shelter beneath it during an unseasonable hailstorm, shivering miserably. Meaning well, she called down that a creature with hands and feet as clever as his ought to build himself a proper house instead of suffering through every cold snap unsheltered. The monkey, irritated by unsolicited advice from a bird far smaller than himself, told her sharply to be quiet -- but she, confident in her own suggestion, kept offering variations of the same advice anyway. Finally, out of patience rather than persuaded, the monkey climbed the tree and tore her nest to pieces.
documents.source_name: The Panchatantra, translated by Arthur W. Ryder (1925)
documents.text:
In a certain wood lived a sparrow and his wife who had built their nest on the branch of a tree. One day in the month of February a monkey took shelter under the tree; for he had been caught in an unseasonable hail-storm, and his body shivered to the slightest breeze. Since his teeth were making music and his face was woebegone and his hands and feet were tightly clenched, the hen-sparrow said to him compassionately: "With hands and feet of human plan, Almost you seem to be a man. So, if you find the weather cool, Why not construct a house, you fool?"

When the monkey heard this, he reflected: "Well, well, some people fancy themselves. Here is this paltry hen-sparrow who has a good opinion of her own judgement..." Thereupon he said to her: "You slut! You wench! You smarty! You needle-face! Be still, Or I will spoil the party; I will, I will, I will."

But she continued to ply him with excellent advice concerning the construction of a house, even after he had thus requested her not to do so. So he climbed the tree and destroyed her nest, breaking it to bits. "And that is why I say: Give counsel only when it fits To such as seek the best. The foolish monkey broke to bits The sparrow's cosy nest."

documents.curated_lesson: A jackal named Supersmart found an elephant that had died naturally, but its hide was too tough for him to tear open alone. A lion arrived, and Supersmart offered the whole carcass as a gift to his king, who, too proud to eat what he hadn't killed, refused and moved on. Next a tiger came, and Supersmart, mixing flattery with fear, spun a story that the lion had killed this elephant and would take vengeance on any tiger who touched it -- the tiger fled. Then a leopard arrived, and Supersmart used friendliness instead, inviting him to eat quickly before the lion returned. The leopard's sharp teeth tore the tough hide open, and the moment the meat was accessible, Supersmart falsely cried that the lion was coming, sending the leopard fleeing too. Only once the hide was open did another jackal arrive, an equal with no reason to be flattered, frightened, or befriended -- so Supersmart simply fought him outright and drove him off, keeping the elephant for himself.
documents.source_name: The Panchatantra, translated by Arthur W. Ryder (1925)
documents.text:
There was once a jackal named Supersmart in a part of a forest. One day he came upon an elephant that had died a natural death in the wood. But he could only stalk about the body; he could not cut through the tough hide.

At this moment a lion... came to the spot. And the jackal... said: "My lord and king, I am merely a cudgel-bearer, guarding this elephant in the king's interest. May the king deign to eat it." Then the lion said: "My good fellow, under no circumstances do I eat what another has killed. I graciously bestow this elephant upon you."

When the lion was gone, a tiger arrived... he said in an agitated tone: "Uncle, how could you venture into the jaws of death? This elephant was killed by a lion, who put me on guard while he went to bathe... 'If any tiger comes this way,' he said, 'creep up and tell me. I have to clear this forest of tigers...'" On hearing this, the tiger was terrified, and said: "My dear nephew, make me a gift of my life... don't give him any news of me." With these words he decamped.

When the tiger had gone, a leopard appeared... "Well, nephew, where have you been this long time?... here lies this elephant, killed by a lion who appointed me its guardian. But for all that, you may enjoy a square meal of elephant-meat, provided you cut and run before he gets back." ... "Don't be timid," said the jackal. "Pluck up courage and eat. I will warn you of his coming while he is yet a long way off." So the leopard did as suggested, and the jackal, as soon as he saw the hide cut through, called out: "Quick, nephew, quick! Here comes the lion." Hearing this, the leopard vanished also.

Now while the jackal was eating meat through the opening cut by the leopard, a second jackal came on the scene in a great rage. And Supersmart, esteeming him an equal whose prowess was a known quantity, recited the stanza: "Sway patrons with obeisance; In heroes raise a doubt; Fling petty bribes to flunkeys; With equals, fight it out" - made a dash at him, tore him with his fangs, made him seek the horizon, and himself comfortably enjoyed elephant-meat for a long time.

documents.curated_lesson: A dog named Spot, driven from his home city by a long famine, traveled to a distant land where he found a careless housewife who left food out generously enough that he could eat his fill every day. But the local dogs, proud and territorial, attacked him savagely each time he left her house, simply because he was an outsider enjoying what they considered their own city's food. Weighing the abundance of food against the daily violence of not belonging, Spot concluded that his own homeland, however famine-struck, was still the better place to live. When he returned home, his relatives gathered eagerly to hear about his travels. Spot's answer captured the whole experience in one wry reply: the food abroad was excellent and the company remarkably easygoing, but the 'relatives' he met there -- the local dogs who should have welcomed a stranger with basic decency -- had no manners at all.
documents.source_name: The Panchatantra, translated by Arthur W. Ryder (1925)
documents.text:
There was once a dog named Spot in a certain town which was afflicted by a long famine. And as food gave out, dogs and others began to lose their homes. In fear of this, Spot felt his throat pinched by hunger, and he went to another country far away. In a city of that country he found a citizen's wife who was slipshod in her housekeeping, so he entered her house every day, and ate his fill from a diversified bill of fare. But as he left the house, other dogs, drunk with aristocratic spleen, closed in from all sides, and tore him in every limb with their fangs.

Then he thought: "Better one's native land, where one lives at peace even in times of famine, and no one picks a quarrel. It is better to return to my own city." Having thus reasoned it through, he returned to his own place.

Then his relatives asked him questions, as one returning from foreign parts: "Come now, tell us about it. What is the country like? How do the people behave? What do they eat? And what are their habits?" And he replied: "Why speak of the country? The food is very good to eat And does not lack variety; While easy-going women meet You in the town's society: But kinsmen in that foreign street Are wanting in sobriety."

documents.story_title: How the Birds Picked a King
documents.curated_lesson: The bird clans, frustrated that their nominal king Garuda paid them no attention and never came to their aid, gathered to choose a real king who would actually protect them. Impressed by his solemn, dignified bearing, they settled unanimously on the owl and began an elaborate coronation ceremony. Just as the ritual was underway, a crow arrived and, curious about the commotion, was invited to give his opinion too, since he was known as the shrewdest of birds. He immediately objected: why crown a creature who is blind precisely during the day, when most danger arrives? Persuaded by this simple but crucial flaw no one else had considered, the birds abandoned the ceremony and flew off to reconsider, leaving the owl alone on his half-finished throne. When the owl learned that the crow's sharp question had cost him the crown, he swore lasting enmity against the crow.
documents.source_name: The Panchatantra, translated by Arthur W. Ryder (1925)
documents.text: There is on a certain mountain a banyan tree, where dwell many birds. Once, when their king Garuda failed to protect them, they assembled and resolved to have another king. "Garuda pays no heed to our sorrows; we suffer death and destruction with no protector; let us choose a king who will guard us in our need." And their eyes falling upon the owl, whose appearance was dignified, they said: "This owl shall be our king." And they made ready with pitchers of holy water, with a throne, with unhusked barley, with oil and lampwicks, with all the paraphernalia of a coronation. And the owl began to be crowned. But at this moment a crow arrived, thinking: "Whither shall birds fly for protection who wish to have such a wry-faced president as this, one who is ugly to see, and ill-tempered even in his everyday moods; how, if angry, would he glare at the person addressing him? And besides, this owl is blind by day. How could he ward off Garuda's attacks upon us, coming as they do in the day?" So he said: "What use is this coronation? Consider: he is hideous of aspect even in a natural state, and how much more so when angry. Blind by day, timid, ill-tempered -- how shall such a king save us from calamity?" Hearing this, the birds cast off their purpose and flew away, leaving the owl on his throne, wondering at their sudden departure.

documents.curated_lesson: A great black snake named Haughty lived in an ant-hill, but one day, rather than take the wide path he normally used to leave his hole, he chose to force his massive body through a much narrower crack -- and in doing so, wounded himself badly. The smell of his blood drew the ants of the hill, who gathered around him in overwhelming numbers. No single ant posed him any threat, but their sheer collective mass, stinging from every side at once, was more than even a powerful snake could withstand. Haughty perished not from any one enemy strong enough to defeat him, but from an uncountable number of small ones acting together.
documents.source_name: The Panchatantra, translated by Arthur W. Ryder (1925)
documents.text: In a certain place there lived a great black snake named Haughty. And one day he thought: "I will not go by the path I have always used, for I am weary of it. I will use a narrower way." So thinking, he crawled with great effort into a very narrow crevice, and in the crush he was severely wounded. And the smell of blood brought a swarm of ants, who stung him from every side. Though he tried to defend himself, killing many, he could not withstand the multitude, and so perished, brought low not by any single powerful foe but by the countless small ones acting together.

documents.curated_lesson: A Brahman farmer, whose land yielded little despite his labor, spotted an imposing snake near an ant-hill and, assuming it was the field's guardian deity gone unhonored, began offering it a saucer of milk every day, receiving a gold coin in return each morning. One day, called away on business, he sent his son to deliver the milk instead. Finding a coin, greed overtook the boy: reasoning the ant-hill must be full of gold, he tried to kill the snake outright, striking it with a club. The snake survived and struck back in self-defense, killing the boy instantly. The grieving father understood his son's own greed, not the snake's nature, had caused the tragedy. Hoping to preserve what remained of the relationship, he returned the next morning with milk as always -- but the snake gave an honest, sobering reply: a funeral pyre can be dismantled and moved, but a heart wounded and patched back together always carries the scar of what happened.
documents.source_name: The Panchatantra, translated by Arthur W. Ryder (1925)
documents.text: In a certain town there lived a Brahman named Haridatta, whose fields yielded little despite his toil. One hot day, resting under a tree, he saw a great snake, hood raised, before an ant-hill nearby, and thought: "This must be the guardian deity of my field, unhonored by me until now; that is why my land does not prosper." So he brought a bowl of milk and offered it, bowing. The next morning he found a gold coin in the bowl's place, and daily thereafter the exchange continued, milk for gold. One day, called away, he sent his son to make the offering. The son, on finding a coin, reasoned that the ant-hill must be full of gold, and resolved to kill the snake and seize the treasure at once. He struck at it with a stick, but the snake escaped the blow and, biting him in self-defense, killed him instantly. The father, grieving, understood that his son's own greed, not the snake's malice, was the cause. Still, hoping to preserve the arrangement, the father returned the next day with the milk as always, and addressed the snake, saying his son had met the fate his own folly deserved, and hoping they might continue as before. But the snake replied: "I will continue the arrangement, since you ask it, but understand: a funeral pyre, once built, can be pulled down and moved; but a heart once wounded, however it is later patched together, retains the scar of the wound. Money you shall have, but never again the trust of former days."

documents.curated_lesson: A king named Gay-Chariot owned a well-guarded lake where golden swans lived, each contributing a valuable tail feather twice a year as a kind of unspoken rent for the protection they received. When a great golden bird arrived seeking to live there too, the resident swans refused him outright, citing their exclusive arrangement with the king. Insulted, the newcomer went straight to the king and reported the swans as rude and inhospitable. The king, without investigating further, angrily ordered his men to kill every bird on the lake. An old swan, spotting the armed men approaching, understood there was no time to argue -- their only chance was to abandon the lake immediately and flee together, which they did just in time to survive. What the swans lost was not their lives, but the home and privileged arrangement they had spent so much effort protecting -- undone in a single day by a refusal of basic hospitality to one guest in need.
documents.source_name: The Panchatantra, translated by Arthur W. Ryder (1925)
documents.text: There was a king named Chitraratha (Gay-Chariot) who owned a lake guarded well, where dwelt golden swans, each of whom, twice a year, gave up a feather of gold as a kind of rent for the protection they enjoyed. One day a great golden bird came seeking to dwell there also, but the resident swans refused him, saying: "This lake is ours by agreement with the king; there is no room here for one who has not shared in our arrangement."
